content: 1. One study was excluded because it was unclear whether the index and reference tests were performed within 30 days. The use of only healthy blood donors was considered a high-risk category, and combined with other unclear factors, this led to a one-point downgrade in the quality of evidence. 2. For the Murex test, three out of four studies had unclear participant selection, but there were no other high-risk concerns for bias. Therefore, no downgrading was applied. 3. Unexplained heterogeneity in the remaining studies may be related to covariates that could not be adjusted for in meta-regression due to limited data, such as HIV and HBV coinfections or HCV genotypes. Additionally, not all studies identified HCV antibody status or stratified by acute and chronic infection, which could contribute to variability in HCV replication and higher false-negative rates for HCV core antigen (HCVcAg). 4. The ARCHITECT studies showed little heterogeneity, so no downgrading was applied. 5. For the Ortho ELISA, moderate heterogeneity was observed, largely due to one outlier study. As a result, one point was downgraded. 6. For the Monolisa sensitivity outcome, heterogeneity between studies precluded meta-analysis, leading to a two-point downgrade. For specificity, only one study was available, preventing an assessment of heterogeneity, and one point was downgraded. 7. For the Murex sensitivity outcome, excessive heterogeneity prevented data pooling, resulting in a two-point downgrade. For specificity, insufficient studies were available for meta-analysis, and heterogeneity could not be formally assessed. However, the broad range of results led to a one-point downgrade. 8. The EIKEN Lumispot was evaluated in only two studies. Sensitivity was consistent across both studies, indicating little heterogeneity, so no downgrading was applied. 9. For the Fujirebio Lumipulse, only one study was available, preventing an assessment of heterogeneity, and one point was downgraded. 10. All studies were conducted in reference laboratories, primarily in highand middle-income countries. This setting is not representative of limited-resource environments for which these guidelines are intended, leading to a one-point downgrade. 11. Imprecision was considered present when pooled confidence intervals exceeded 10% or when fewer than 250 samples were included in the analysis. Consequently, the Ortho ELISA and Hunan Jynda were downgraded one point for wide confidence intervals, and the Lumispot was downgraded one point for small sample size. Imprecision could not be graded for the Monolisa specificity outcome or the Lumipulse test due to the inclusion of only one study. 12. HCV is a small, enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Flaviviridae family, with seven genotypes and over 67 subtypes. Its genome is contained within an internal capsid formed by three domains of the HCV core protein, which is highly conserved and antigenic. During viral assembly, nucleocapsid peptides (p22) are released into plasma and can be detected early in the course of infection. 13. Screening assays for anti-HCV antibodies (HCV Ab) were among the first diagnostic tools developed to identify HCV infection. However, they only indicate exposure to the virus and not active replication or ongoing infection. The serological window for conversion to a positive antibody test is highly variable, averaging 60 days. Antibodies may remain persistently negative in patients on hemodialysis, those with poorly controlled HIV infection, or other immunocompromised states. 14. Diagnosis of active HCV infection requires antibody testing followed by an assessment for viremia to confirm true infection in antibody-positive patients and to identify high-risk antibody-negative patients. Confirmatory testing can be based on nucleic acid testing (NAT) to detect HCV RNA or antigen testing to detect core antigen. 15. HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) tests, primarily targeting p22, have been developed as an alternative to NAT since their initial demonstration in 1995. The first commercial assay was released in 2000. HCVcAg tests have the potential to be less costly and less centralized than NAT. 16. Detection of HCV viremia is also important during the treatment of chronic HCV infection. Current guidelines recommend virological confirmation pretreatment with baseline viral load measurement using NAT. For interferon-based treatments, viral load is assessed at week 4 of therapy to predict efficacy and guide treatment continuation. NAT is repeated at week 12, at the end of treatment, and 12 and 24 weeks post-therapy to confirm cure (sustained virological response, SVR). 17. With the advent of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), NAT during therapy may no longer be necessary. DAAs have also made HCV treatment accessible in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing the need for affordable diagnostic and monitoring tests. 18. This systematic review aims to assess the diagnostic accuracy of HCVcAg testing for HCV detection and to inform the best testing strategy for identifying chronic HCV infection. Additionally, the review evaluates the utility of HCVcAg for monitoring HCV treatment and testing for cure. 19. Only commercially available tests were included in this systematic review. The most widely studied test is the Abbott ARCHITECT HCV Ag assay, a two-step automated chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) for quantitative determination of HCVcAg in serum or plasma. Other tests include the Fujirebio Lumipulse, Ortho HCV Ag test, EIKEN Lumispot, Murex HCV Ag-Ab combination, and Bio-Rad Monolisa HCV Ag-Ab ULTRA. Two ELISA-based HCVcAg tests, the Hunan Jynda Bioengineering Group HCV Core Ag ELISA and Ortho ELISA-Ag, were also included.
